summary: Extends the OAuth 2.0 framework with request parameters that let a client tell the authorization server which protected resource or resources it wants access to. The server can then issue tokens suited to those resources.

plainLanguage.summary: An OAuth client usually knows which API it wants to reach, but the authorization server has no standard way to be told. RFC 8707 adds a resource parameter for that, so the server can build a token for that API and make the token valid only there.

questions: what is the oauth resource parameter
how to audience restrict an oauth access token
subtitle: A request parameter that lets an OAuth client say which API a requested access token is meant for.

tldr.problem: An OAuth authorization server often does not know where a client will use the access token it requests, so it cannot build the token for that resource or limit where the token works.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds one or more resource parameters, each an absolute URI naming the target resource, to authorization and token requests. The server can then restrict the token to that audience and use the invalid_target error for values it will not accept.
tldr.outcome: Tokens can be made valid only at the intended resources, so a resource that receives a token cannot reuse it to reach a different one. The RFC also warns that a token with several audiences is trusted by every one of them.

facts.label: Audience carried in
facts.value: The aud claim or the top-level aud member

facts.label: Multiple values allowed
facts.value: Yes, but a single resource is encouraged

today: RFC 8707 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2020. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so the resource parameter remains the registered way to tell an authorization server which protected resource an access token is meant for.

sections.title: Why a Client Names Its Target Resource
sections.content:
Deployment and implementation experience with the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749) has uncovered a need, in some circumstances such as an authorization server serving a large number of diverse resources, for the client to signal explicitly where it intends to use the access token it is requesting.

Knowing the protected resource, also called the resource server, application or API, lets the authorization server construct the token the way that entity needs it. Encrypting a token, or content inside it, to a particular resource requires knowing which resource will receive and decrypt it. Different resources also have different requirements about the data contained in or referenced by the token, and knowing the intended resource lets the server mint the token accordingly.

Knowing the intended recipients also improves the security of the token. Bearer tokens, currently the most common type of OAuth access token, allow any party in possession of the token to access the associated resources, so several security assumptions have to hold. One is that an access token is valid only for use at a specific protected resource and for a specific scope of access. Section 5.2 of RFC 6750 prescribes including the token's intended recipients within the token to prevent token redirect.

OAuth scope is sometimes overloaded to convey the location or identity of the protected resource, but that is not always feasible or desirable. Scope values in use in the wild, such as email, admin:org, user_photos, channels:read and channels:write, describe the type of access being requested rather than where that access will be redeemed. A number of implementations have already used proprietary parameters for this purpose, and this specification provides a standardized and interoperable alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: An OAuth client often knows which API it wants to use, but the authorization server has no standard way to be told. This RFC adds a resource parameter so the server can build a token for that API, and can make the token valid only there.

sections.title: The resource Parameter
sections.content:
In a request to the authorization server, a client MAY include a resource parameter indicating the protected resource to which access is being requested. Its value MUST be an absolute URI, and the URI MUST NOT include a fragment component. It SHOULD NOT include a query component, but the RFC recognizes cases where a query component is a useful and necessary part of the parameter, such as when one or more query parameters are used to scope requests to an application. The value is an identifier representing the identity of the resource, and it MAY be a locator that corresponds to a network-addressable location where the target resource is hosted. Multiple resource parameters MAY be used to indicate that the requested token is intended for several resources.

The client SHOULD provide the most specific URI it can for the complete API or set of resources it intends to access. In practice a client knows a base URI for the application it interacts with, and SHOULD use the base URI of the API as the value unless specific knowledge of the resource dictates otherwise. For an application that is the exclusive one on a host, the value https://api.example.com/ would be used; if the host serves many applications, something like https://api.example.com/app/ is more specific. The RFC gives the SCIM API (RFC 7644) as an example of an API with several endpoints, where a client would use https://apps.example.com/scim/ so that the issued token is valid for all of them.

The authorization server SHOULD audience-restrict issued access tokens to the resource or resources named in the parameter. Audience restrictions can be communicated in JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519) with the aud claim, and a top-level member of the same name provides the audience restriction information in a token introspection (RFC 7662) response. The server may use the exact resource value as the audience, or map it to a more general URI or abstract identifier for the resource.

One error code is provided so the server can report a problem with the requested resources, including a combination of resource and scope the server will not accept. The code is invalid_target, whose value says that the requested resource is invalid, missing, unknown or malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter value is an absolute address of the target API, with no fragment part. The client should be as specific as it can. The server then restricts the token to that API, and answers invalid_target when it cannot accept the value.

sections.title: The Parameter in an Authorization Request
sections.content:
When the resource parameter is used in an authorization request to the authorization endpoint, it indicates the identity of the protected resource or resources to which access is being requested. If an access token is returned directly from the authorization endpoint through the implicit flow, the requested resource applies to that access token. In the code flow, where an intermediate representation of the authorization grant, the authorization code, is returned from the authorization endpoint, the requested resource applies to the full authorization grant.

In an authorization request sent as a JSON Web Token, such as when using the JWT Secured Authorization Request, a single resource parameter value is represented as a JSON string, while multiple values are represented as an array of strings.

If the client omits the parameter, the authorization server MAY process the request with no specific resource or with a predefined default resource value. Alternatively it MAY require clients to specify the resources they intend to access, and MAY fail requests that omit the parameter with an invalid_target error. The server might use this data to inform the user about the resources the client is going to access on their behalf, to apply policy such as refusing the request because of an unknown resource, and to determine the set of resources usable in later access token requests. If the server fails to parse the provided values, or does not consider the resources acceptable, it should reject the request with an error response using invalid_target as the value of the error parameter, and can give the reasons in error_description.
sections.plainLanguage: In an authorization request the parameter names the API the client wants to reach. If the client leaves it out, the server may use a default, or may refuse the request with an error. The server also uses the value to tell the user which resources the client will reach on their behalf.

sections.title: The Parameter in a Token Request
sections.content:
On an access token request made to the token endpoint, for all grant types, the resource parameter indicates the target service or protected resource where the client intends to use the requested access token. The resource values that are acceptable to an authorization server are at its sole discretion, based on local policy or configuration. For a refresh_token or authorization_code grant, that policy may limit the acceptable resources to those originally granted by the resource owner or a subset of them. In the authorization_code case where the requested resources are a subset of the resources originally granted, the authorization server issues an access token based on that subset, whereas any refresh token that is returned is bound to the full original grant.

The client asks for a token with the requested scope that is usable at all the requested target services. The requested access rights of the token are effectively the cartesian product of all the scopes at all the target services. To the extent possible, when issuing access tokens, the authorization server should downscope the scope value associated with an access token to the value the respective resource is able to process and needs to know. Downscoping means giving fewer permissions than the resource owner originally authorized. It further improves privacy, because a list of scope values indicates that the resource owner uses several services, and a token scoped to what one service needs limits how much of that is revealed across services. As required by Section 5.1 of RFC 6749, the authorization server must indicate the access token's effective scope to the client in the scope response parameter value when it differs from the scope the client requested.
sections.plainLanguage: On a token request the parameter again names the API the token is meant for, and the server may narrow the permissions to what that API actually needs. Asking for several APIs in one token is allowed, but then the token works at all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An audience-restricted access token that is legitimately presented to a resource cannot then be taken by that resource and presented elsewhere for illegitimate access to other resources. The resource parameter enables a client to indicate the protected resources where the requested access token will be used, which in turn enables the authorization server to apply the appropriate audience restrictions to the token.

Some servers host user content or are multi-tenant. To avoid attacks where one tenant uses an access token to reach resources owned by a different tenant, it is important to use a specific resource URI that includes any portion of the URI identifying the tenant, such as a path component. That allows access tokens to be audience-restricted in a way that identifies the tenant and prevents their use, due to an invalid audience, at resources owned by a different tenant.

Although multiple occurrences of the parameter may be included in a token request, using only a single resource parameter is encouraged. A bearer token with multiple intended recipients is valid at more than one protected resource, and it can be used by any one of those resources to access any of the others, so a high degree of trust between the involved parties is needed. An authorization server may also be unwilling or unable to fulfil a token request with multiple resources.

Whenever feasible the parameter should correspond to the network-addressable location of the protected resource. That makes it possible for the client to validate that the resource being requested controls the corresponding network location, reducing the risk of malicious endpoints obtaining tokens meant for other resources. If the parameter contains an abstract identifier, it is the client's responsibility to validate out of band that any network endpoint to which tokens are sent is the intended audience for that identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A token that is only good at one API cannot be handed to that API and reused at another. Name one resource rather than several, and include the tenant in the URI when the server hosts more than one, so a token from one tenant cannot be used at another tenant's resources.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content: In typical OAuth deployments the authorization server is in a position to observe and track a significant amount of user and client behaviour. That is largely inherent in the nature of OAuth, and this document does little to affect it. In some cases, however, such as when access token introspection is not being used, the resource parameter may allow tracking of behaviour at a more granular and specific level than would otherwise be possible in its absence.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization server already sees a lot about what people do. Naming the resource adds a little more detail about which services a person uses, mostly when the server does not use token introspection.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers two names with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. The parameter resource is added to the IANA "OAuth Parameters" registry, with its usage location listed as authorization request and token request, and the change controller listed as the IESG. The error invalid_target is added to the IANA "OAuth Extensions Error Registry", with its usage location listed as implicit grant error response and token error response, its related protocol extension named as the resource parameter, and the change controller listed as the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers the parameter name and the error name in the IANA registries, so that other specifications use the same spelling.
